overview: Proto-Tibetan cultures is an atlas label, not a name recovered from people between 400 and 323 BCE. Its single enormous polygon covers central and eastern plateau valleys, Qaidam, much of Tarim, Kashgar, Kathmandu, and Lumbini, while excluding Ngari and Ladakh. That shape is an editorial umbrella, not a language map, frontier, state, or census. Archaeology offers smaller stories. Central Tibetan communities at Bangga combined barley farming, herding, storage, houses, and corrals. Western plateau grain isotopes show intensive crop care, while Mebrak and Kyang in the High Himalayas preserve communal burials, children, textiles, animals, health clues, and long-distance objects. These places differed, and none proves everyone inside the polygon spoke one reconstructed ancestor language. Family organization, teaching, healing, water use, and waste practices are described where evidence allows. The dates divide a short teaching window through evidence spanning broader ranges; no event is invented per decade. No securely attested writing survives from this people and interval. The atlas id disappears at 323 BCE, yet local communities, skills, exchange, speech, and settlement continued without a matching collapse.

periods.title: 400 to 390 BCE: the atlas umbrella appears
periods.summary: The exact id first appears in the 400 BCE snapshot. Mebrak cave use also begins around 400 BCE within a much broader archaeological region. This decade is a teaching slice, not evidence that one people was founded everywhere inside the polygon at once.

periods.title: 390 to 380 BCE: local settlement evidence stays local
periods.summary: Bangga and surveyed central Tibetan sites show first-millennium BCE agropastoral settlement and seasonal landscape use. Their broad dates overlap this slice, but the research does not securely isolate a ten-year transformation or extend one household pattern across the atlas shape.

periods.title: 380 to 370 BCE: herding required active provisioning
periods.summary: Sheep and goat teeth from Bangga record water, fodder, and grazing choices across a broad 3000 to 2200 BP occupation. The evidence alone supports skilled herd care during this atlas window, without pinpointing a change specifically in these ten years.

periods.title: 370 to 360 BCE: barley fields demanded labor
periods.summary: Western Tibetan barley isotopes indicate watering and manuring during a long first-millennium BCE to first-millennium CE span. This teaching slice represents overlapping practice, not a dated invention in 370 BCE or one recipe widely shared across many different plateau communities.

periods.title: 360 to 350 BCE: crop systems remained dynamic
periods.summary: Bangga archaeobotanical evidence spans about 1055 to 211 BCE and traces movement toward barley dominance. The interval overlaps that long process. It does not prove that wheat vanished, that every meal used barley, or that a single policy directed farming.

periods.title: 350 to 340 BCE: burial preserves social choices unevenly
periods.summary: Mebrak mortuary evidence includes communal placement, wooden platforms, textiles, animals, beads, and other goods within a long cave-use phase. These finds reveal care and connection, while leaving household rules, rank, and belief systems open. No text explains their precise meanings.

periods.title: 340 to 330 BCE: language remains a model, not a label
periods.summary: Linguistic reconstruction can test histories of related speech, but archaeological similarity does not directly identify a spoken language. Nothing securely ties the full atlas polygon to one Proto-Tibetan speech community during this teaching slice. Speech likely varied across communities and routes.

periods.title: 330 to 323 BCE: the software window closes
periods.summary: The target disappears at the 323 BCE snapshot, with no matching destruction layer, conquest, or mass departure in the reviewed evidence. This seven-year slice ends the atlas record only; regional communities and changing lifeways continued. No society simply disappears here.

sections.title: Decode a very strange atlas umbrella

items.text: The exact index record is a circa culture dated 400 to 323 BCE, generated from historical basemaps. Coverage finds one matching border interval and no card. Those are database facts about this missing entry; they are not proof that ancient residents used the modern label Proto-Tibetan cultures.

Only world-bc400 contains the id. Its decoded Polygon has one ring, 31 positions, and bounds from roughly 72.78 to 104.32 degrees east and 25.62 to 43.31 degrees north. A tidy single outline here is a cartographic convenience, not an excavated boundary stone.

Point tests place Lhasa, Yarlung, Shigatse, Nagqu, Chamdo, Nyingchi, Qaidam, Hotan, central Tarim, Kashgar, Kathmandu, and Lumbini inside. Ngari, Kyunglung, Leh, Lanzhou, Aba, Chengdu, and Kunming fall outside today. That peculiar selection defeats any simple ethnic, ecological, or linguistic reading.

The target shares encoded arcs with atlas regions labeled Achaemenid Empire, Hindu Kingdoms, Xiongnu, Zhangzhung Kingdom, Magadha, proto-Thai cultures, and Austro-Asiatic rice cultures. Those seams reveal how the basemap was patched together. They do not document treaties, guarded borders, or seven simultaneous diplomatic neighbors.

The earlier Tibetans record ends at 500 BCE, this id begins at 400 BCE, and the target disappears at 323 BCE. The intervening gap and label changes are software chronology. This card therefore has no automatic predecessor or successor and does not turn three atlas names into one timeless population.

Plateau archaeology remains geographically uneven, so regional syntheses compare dated settlements, burials, plants, animals, tools, and landscapes without claiming complete coverage. A find from Mustang can illuminate one Himalayan corridor, while a Bangga corral illuminates central Tibet. Neither automatically fills Kashgar or Lumbini merely because the polygon does.

Central Tibet surveys combine pedestrian work, shovel tests, drone mapping, GIS, radiocarbon dating, and ceramic composition. Yukang and Badong appear to have been used seasonally, a conclusion built from several methods. Even so, seasonal use at two sites does not describe every family in every mapped valley.

Stable carbon and nitrogen isotope values in ancient barley help researchers infer water and soil management. This is clever chemistry, but it works on sampled grains from particular sites. It cannot identify a farmer's name, field owner, spoken language, or exact instructions passed between generations.

Sequential carbon and oxygen isotope measurements along sheep and goat teeth can track seasonal food and drinking-water patterns. Researchers compare those signals with local environments and herding possibilities. The result is a tested reconstruction, not a tiny livestock diary helpfully filed under the year 372 BCE.

High Himalayan researchers combine radiocarbon dates, genomes, isotopes, bones, teeth, artifacts, and climate models. Agreement among methods strengthens an interpretation, while disagreement exposes uncertainty. The evidence can show population connections and adaptation without assigning one ancient ethnicity to all people buried at Mebrak and Kyang.

sections.title: Live in houses, tend fields, and eat

items.text: Bangga research identifies a settled agropastoral community in the first millennium BCE, while nearby surveyed highland corrals may reflect seasonal use. Permanent homes and mobile herding could coexist within one regional system. That mix is more realistic than forcing every household into either a wandering or completely sedentary box.

Bangga plant remains span a long sequence from about 1055 to 211 BCE and show movement toward barley dominance. The transition was gradual and locally studied. Barley mattered enormously, but dominance in recovered grains does not mean that every person ate identical porridge at every meal.

Western plateau grain isotopes suggest communities manured barley and, at Piyang and Jiweng, supplied additional water or chose moisture-retaining soils. Dingdong shows a different watering signal. Those differences reveal active decisions adapted to place, rather than one prehistoric instruction manual circulating unchanged across every high valley.

At Bangga, stone-built domestic features, hearths, postholes, pits, storage areas, and nearby corrals show daily work concentrated around built spaces. Barley and other plants complemented herds. The surviving layout supports cooking, storage, and shelter, while bedding, furniture, recipes, and room assignments remain mostly invisible.

A long southern plateau record links people with changing drought conditions, cultivation, and pastoral adjustments. Adaptation meant revising practices rather than conquering altitude once and forever. Climate evidence provides a regional backdrop, but it cannot explain each harvest, household move, hungry winter, or lucky rainy season by itself.

Bangga sheep and goats may have received groundwater and agricultural fodder, with summer grazing in saline or marshy areas. That pattern suggests intensive provisioning at high elevation. It also shows that pastoralism involved careful schedules and resources, not simply opening a gate and hoping the flock had excellent navigation.

Age-at-death patterns among Bangga caprines have been tested against specialized culling and high natural lamb mortality. The analysis makes herd management visible while preserving uncertainty. Bones can record which ages died; they rarely tell whether weather, disease, labor goals, or several pressures shaped every loss.

Survey work beneath and around modern corrals found prehistoric pastoral sites at Yukang and Badong. Repeated use of mountain places can create durable pathways and knowledge. Researchers model such landscapes carefully, because a corral's location does not reveal the names, kin groups, ownership rules, or full route of its users.

Landscape and network models compare vegetation routes, settlements, and ceramic similarities across Tibet. The models suggest relationships among mobility and social interaction, especially in eastern areas, but remain analytical tools. Herders made situated choices that no least-cost line can fully recover, including stops caused by weather, births, illness, or negotiation.

Mebrak and Kyang evidence points to successful life at high altitude through biological traits, local practices, and exchange networks. No single factor deserves all the credit. Adaptation was social as well as bodily, and communities could connect across mountains without becoming one population, household pattern, or political unit.

Tibetan metal finds include copper, bronze, iron, and composite objects, with evidence for several technological routes. The record around the early Metal Age is complex and uneven. An iron ornament or weapon shows skilled production and exchange, not a migrating ethnic label conveniently attached to the object's alloy.

Mebrak's communal cave preserved finely woven textiles, wooden objects, pottery, ornaments, and human and animal remains. Twenty-eight radiocarbon samples place use around 400 BCE to 50 CE. The unusual preservation opens a vivid window, though grave goods are not a complete inventory of ordinary household possessions.

Mustang's Kali Gandaki valley links the plateau and Indian plains. Archaeologists find modeled gray pottery, cord-impressed vessels, and funerary caves, while stressing how few sites have been excavated. Connections moved objects and ideas through this corridor, but sparse evidence cannot reconstruct a scheduled ancient delivery service.

Mebrak grave goods include textiles made from several fibers, beads, bronze ornaments, carved wooden platforms, and painted animal images. These objects demonstrate material skill and wide connections. Their presence among the dead may express remembrance or status, yet no single meaning applies automatically to every object or burial.

Bangga's changing crop assemblage records technical choices as ecological and social conditions shifted. Seed selection, soil preparation, harvesting, storage, and cooking all required practiced knowledge even when individuals remain unnamed. Agricultural achievement here is cumulative expertise, not a sudden invention credited to one ruler or one neatly bounded culture.

sections.title: Keep family and social life evidence-sized

items.text: Mebrak's demographic study includes adults and subadults, allowing researchers to ask who entered the burial chamber. A cemetery shows that children and adults belonged to remembered communities, but death assemblages are selective. They cannot reveal a complete living household, marriage rule, residence pattern, or family tree.

Older Mebrak burials were moved aside as new bodies entered the communal chamber, and later disturbance also altered remains. Repeated access suggests sustained social responsibility for the dead. It does not identify exactly which relatives returned, who made decisions, or whether every nearby family used this cave.

Genomic results connect early High Himalayan people with plateau ancestry while South Asian objects appear in mortuary settings. Ancestry, objects, and identity therefore did not travel as one package. Families could participate in exchange and migration without becoming reducible to either a modern national category or the atlas polygon.

Variation among early plateau and Himalayan graves includes body treatment, animals, platforms, containers, and furnishings. Difference may relate to age, status, community, sequence, or beliefs, but the evidence seldom chooses one explanation. Social life was structured; archaeology cannot safely turn every burial contrast into a permanent class rule.

Mustang's protohistory is known disproportionately through funerary remains, with settlement evidence much less secure. That imbalance matters: the dead may be more archaeologically visible than ordinary days. Reconstructing family life therefore requires modest claims, because tombs preserve ceremonies better than arguments, jokes, chores, affection, or sleeping arrangements.

sections.title: Let children learn without inventing schools

items.text: Mebrak includes ten studied subadults, and skeletal researchers record childhood stress indicators where preservation permits. Children were present in these communities, not historical scenery. Their remains cannot tell us their names, games, favorite foods, chores, or whether age categories matched modern childhood divisions.

A naturally preserved child from Mebrak is dated to the fourth century BCE, directly inside this card's window. The find confirms a child's place in the mortuary record and deserves care. It does not authorize a dramatic biography, cause of death, costume story, or universal childhood custom.

Growing and processing barley required observation, timing, and repeated practice. Archaeobotany shows changing technical knowledge, although it does not record a lesson. Children likely learned within daily work, but that is a bounded inference. No exact-period school, textbook, formal curriculum, or standard graduation age is documented.

Reconstructing Proto-Tibetan means comparing later language evidence to propose earlier forms and changes. It does not recover a recording of what a particular child said in 350 BCE. Spoken learning surely occurred, yet the teacher, setting, multilingual context, and words used by these archaeological communities remain unknown.

A proto-language is, by definition, reconstructed from descendant evidence rather than directly attested in surviving text. Stars placed before reconstructed forms mark scholarly status, not an ancient spelling convention. That distinction keeps an educational card honest: a clever modern reconstruction is not prehistoric homework found in a cave.

Mebrak teeth preserve evidence of caries, tooth loss, wear, and abscesses. Researchers compare patterns by age and sex while accounting for missing or damaged remains. Dental disease can illuminate food and bodily experience; it does not identify the treatment used, the healer consulted, or whether pain relief succeeded.

Childhood stress markers at Mebrak are studied through teeth and bones, and their overall frequencies are interpreted carefully. Low visible stress does not equal an easy childhood, perfect nutrition, or freedom from illness. Many problems leave no skeletal trace, while preservation and survival shape who enters the sample.

Across Mebrak and Kyang, low frequencies of nonspecific stress and trauma support successful high-altitude adaptation, possibly buffered by exchange and local practices. That conclusion concerns population patterns. It cannot diagnose every individual, and it does not reveal exact remedies, birth assistance, caregiving roles, or ritual specialists.

Human remains, animal offerings, textiles, and containers in Mebrak graves show sustained care for bodies after death. Mortuary care is visible; medical care during life is much harder to recover. The card therefore does not name herbs, surgeons, shamans, or cures unless an exact-period source actually documents them.

High lamb mortality at Bangga reminds us that people managed animal illness, weather risk, birth seasons, and loss as part of subsistence. Faunal data reveal pressures on herds, not human diagnoses. They cannot prove that animal remedies doubled as medicines for children or that one specialist treated both.

sections.title: Follow water, dung, waste, and missing toilets

items.text: Barley isotope results suggest added water at Piyang and Jiweng, while Dingdong relied less on supplementation. Water management varied even among western highland sites. The evidence concerns crops, not drinking pipes, bathing rules, or sewage. Irrigation skill should not be drafted into the job of an undocumented bathroom system.

Bangga animal teeth suggest livestock sometimes drank groundwater and grazed in saline or marshy places. That is evidence about herd provisioning, not human drinking-water safety. People certainly needed water, but the study does not identify wells, filtration, boiling, household containers, or rules for separating animals and people.

Mebrak's dry cave preserved bodies, textiles, wood, and other materials unusually well, while movement and nesting birds disturbed the chamber. Preservation can make one place seem richer than ordinary settlements. It does not mean people lived in the burial room or handled daily rubbish and human waste there.

Bangga structures, corrals, hearths, pits, and ceramics support domestic and pastoral activity, but no reviewed exact-period publication identifies a latrine or sewer for this atlas umbrella. That absence is not proof of careless hygiene. Toilets are shy archaeologically, especially when organic traces and lightweight screens disappear.

Drought records show why water availability mattered across generations, while local communities adjusted cultivation and herding. Environmental pressure can shape daily routines without dictating one response. The evidence does not recover who fetched water, how vessels were cleaned, where people relieved themselves, or how privacy was organized.

sections.title: Handle language, belief, achievement, and continuity

items.text: Written-language sample: none securely attributable to these communities between 400 and 323 BCE. The earliest corpus collected by Old Tibetan Documents Online belongs to the seventh through twelfth centuries CE. Printing its script here would jump roughly a millennium and falsely assign later imperial-era writing to an archaeological umbrella.

Old Tibetan Documents Online contains manuscripts, inscriptions, and edited texts, but all are later than this card. They are excellent evidence for another era. The missing exact-period sample is itself important: pots, graves, crops, genes, and reconstructed words cannot be silently converted into a local inscription.

Proto-Tibetan forms are modern comparative reconstructions, not spellings copied from 350 BCE. Scholars can debate sound changes and relationships using later languages and texts. The card therefore shows no starred word as a written sample and does not assume that everyone inside the polygon spoke one ancestral variety.

Mebrak animal remains, painted platforms, grave goods, and repeated communal burial imply meaningful treatment of the dead. They do not securely name deities, priests, prayers, or one religion. Respectful interpretation stops before importing later Bon, Buddhist, Hindu, or local traditions backward into a fourth-century BCE cave.

The lasting achievement visible here is adaptive expertise: intensive barley care, skilled herd provisioning, built settlements, crafted textiles and metal, mountain exchange, and sustained remembrance of the dead. These accomplishments belonged to varied local communities. The atlas endpoint removes a label, while the knowledge behind those practices continued and changed.

ending.text: The 323 BCE endpoint is the atlas record's software boundary, not a documented conquest, migration, or collapse. The sole enormous feature disappears under this id, while adjacent atlas regions persist or change separately. Local communities, languages, fields, herds, families, crafts, exchange, and mortuary traditions continued through their own histories beyond this short editorial window.
